articles.title: Karl review – straightforward tribute tells inside story of fashion world’s great eccentric Karl Lagerfeld
articles.summary: Based on Lagerfeld’s biography, director Nick Hooker gets access to the designer’s inner circle, but ultimately fails to find the man behind the high collar and sunglasses.
body: Karl Lagerfeld had never set foot inside a supermarket before he had one built on a catwalk in 2014, featuring models browsing aisles with baskets shopping for Chanel-branded fromage. It was classic Lagerfeld: very silly but a stroke of genius. The fashion designer was easy to poke fun at, with his white bouffant-plus-ponytail hairstyle and black leather gloves. But behind the persona was a man who spoke four languages fluently, a workaholic still running Chanel, Fendi and his own label Karl Lagerfeld into his 80s.

This dutiful, uncontroversial documentary is based on William Middleton’s biography Paradise Now: The Extraordinary Life of Karl Lagerfeld. As well as archive footage of Lagerfeld, film-maker Nick Hooker gets access to the designer’s inner circle, but ultimately his documentary fails to chip away at the persona. (This is no criticism: I once interviewed Lagerfeld, a frustrating 30 minutes during which the dark glasses stayed on and he answered questions with bon mot witticisms but gave nothing away.) In a clip at the start of the film, Lagerfeld admits that he has spent so long performing a role that not even those closest to him really know who he is.
points: Based on Lagerfeld’s biography, director Nick Hooker gets access to the designer’s inner circle, but ultimately fails to find the man behind the high collar and sunglasses.

articles.title: France’s Canal+ Threatens to Pull $1.1 Billion Cinema Deal Over French Tax Hike
articles.summary: Canal+ Group chairman Maxime Saada has warned that the pay TV banner could pull out of its €1 billion ($1.1 billion) investment deal with the French film industry if the government goes ahead with plans to double VAT on pay-TV subscriptions.
body: The suggested change in VAT, which is included in the government’s proposed finance bill, would cost Canal+ Group approximately €200 million per year.

Saada said during an interview with French radio RTL that the change would effectively void Canal+’s existing agreement with French film organizations, under which the group has committed to invest roughly €1 billion in in French and European films between 2028 and 2032.

“We invest more in cinema than any other player. Our commitment to film organizations is a contract, and the first clause – the quid pro quo for Canal+’s funding of cinema — is the reduced VAT rate,” Saada said. “We don’t even need to renegotiate it. The contract is void if the standard VAT rate is applied.”
If Canal+ were to fall back on its strict regulatory obligations rather than maintain its current commitments, its annual contribution to cinema could drop to around €50 million, according to Saada.

articles.title: The Yellow Tie review – John Malkovich gives major hauteur as legendary record-hating maestro
articles.summary: This biopic of Sergiu Celibidache, the renowned Romanian conductor who refused all recordings, is a sturdy labour of love directed by his son. Here is an old-fashioned biopic from central Europe that is also a labour of love on the part of its director: a little stolid and stately, yes, but…
body: Celibidache studies in Berlin in the 1930s as the Nazis take power, and is menaced and bullied as a Jew, but escapes the ultimate fate; he is sensationally installed as principal conductor of the newly denazified Berlin Philharmonic in 1945, where he astonishes the authorities with his no-recording views. He is finally forced out and begins a kind of wandering musical odyssey through Europe and Latin America.

It is not easy to see what point exactly has been made by Celebidache’s stand; he did not appear to accumulate many followers, and the music world was filled with musicians at least as talented and principled as him who believed the exact opposite about recorded music. But there is a kind of lonely heroism here, and who can tell if, in this digitised world where recordings are so easily available, that his views might not come into fashion? A strong, unassuming picture.

articles.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor Taking Legal Action Against Police Over Search Warrants in Arrest
articles.summary: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, the former prince and King Charles’ brother, is taking legal action against the Thames Valley Police over search warrants relating to his February arrest.
body: A private court hearing will be held on Thursday to consider Mountbatten-Windsor’s request.

Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested by the Thames Valley Police on Feb. 19, his 66th birthday, in relation to their investigation into a a complaint that alleged the former prince had shared confidential material with the late, disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein. He was later released under investigation.

Mountbatten-Windsor was stripped of his royal title last year over his ties to Epstein, and was mentioned and pictured many times in the over 3 million pages of the Epstein files, which were released by the U.S. Department of Justice in February. The former prince, who had a longtime friendship with Epstein and maintained contact with him after his 2008 conviction of procuring a child for prostitution, has previously apologized and denied any wrongdoing.

body: John de Mol ’s Talpa Studios, whose hit formats include quiz show “The Floor,” is heading to next week’s TV market Mipcom with a slate of new entertainment formats, led by “Sing With Me” and “The Golden Elevators.”
“The Golden Elevators,” a quiz show that combines general knowledge with social strategy, has been ordered by ITV in the U.K. and SBS6 in the Netherlands, where it is set to air early next year.

Ten contestants enter a skyscraper where they must choose between two elevators, each representing a possible answer to 10 questions. Choose correctly and you go up; choose the wrong one and you’re out.

Before the doors close, contestants may work together and share what they know – or deliberately send a rival into the wrong elevator – turning every question into a battle of knowledge, strategy and trust. Waiting at the top is a life-changing jackpot, to share with whoever makes it there.

articles.title: Charlie Shaw’s Revenge review – creepy clown killer takes aim at struggling amusement park
articles.summary: Decent effects and a late-stage twist show promise, but this gore-fest needs to be more disgusting, funny or unnerving. The film opens with a lone figure striding into the foreground. He’s an amateur entertainer on his way to a gig, and he’s not been met at the station as planned.
body: Horror movies don’t have to be scary, of course – some get away with just being disgusting, or funny, or unnerving. Unfortunately, Charlie Shaw’s Revenge doesn’t hit any of these marks, either. Its most successful element is a late-stage twist, which works pretty well, though it will feel familiar to viewers of a certain 2003 French slasher. If this was a student’s graduation project, it would show promise – but judged by the standards of professional entertainment, this is, alas, well under par.

articles.title: Digger may lose $150m after Tom Cruise film bombs at the box office
articles.summary: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s critically panned satire took just $20m globally in its opening weekend, against a reported $150m production budget and $100m marketing spend. Digger has flopped in its opening weekend with a $20m global box office, handing Tom Cruise one of the worst debuts of his career and…
body: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s critically panned satire grossed a paltry $8m at the North American box office. Cruise is typically a big draw overseas, but international sales – $12m from 74 markets – were also weak.

It is a rough start for a movie that cost at least $125m to make. Reports have pegged the production budget closer to $150m, while the marketing spend is estimated at another $100m. After reviews so bad that Warner Bros opted to run “decide for yourself” ads, estimates for Digger had been revised down over the past week.

No 1 in North American theaters instead went to Amazon MGM’s Verity, which debued with $32.6m, extending the streak for Colleen Hoover adaptations at the box office. The Michael Showalter-directed film stars Dakota Johnson as a writer hired to ghostwrite a book series by an incapacitated author, played by Anne Hathaway.

articles.title: Charity tea room may close despite Ludwig filming
articles.summary: The series, starring David Mitchell, is filming scenes in Hemel Hempstead.
body: A tea room being used to film the third series of comedy drama Ludwig could close permanently unless it raises £25,000.
Trustees of the volunteer-run Liberty Tea Rooms and Community Hub in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, said the charity was in an "extremely low cash position".
Mark Kitson, chairman of the trustees, said the series being filmed at the venue had created a real buzz and it had been good to hire it out "at a time that we really need the extra funds".

The tea room is temporarily closed until 7 October while filming takes place for the BBC series, which stars David Mitchell. Its frontage has been transformed to resemble a bank, which it was before becoming a community venue.

articles.title: Movies With “Real Political Messages” Underneath the Surface, Animation and More: What Not to Miss at London Film Fest
articles.summary: Kristy Matheson previews key highlights and stars featured in the 70th edition and why she doesn't agree with people having "a grumble about how it doesn't seem like a big or a good year for cinema."
body: More than 250 films from long-time festival favorites and new and emerging voices will screen at the 70th edition of the BFI London Film Festival (LFF), which kicks off on Wednesday. Among them are such high-profile world premieres of animated movies Ray Gunn by Brad Bird and Wildwood by Travis Knight.

Matheson talked to THR about this edition’s selection, stars and possible surprises, and what not to miss this year. With the 70th edition being a big, round number, did you and your team feel the need to do anything special for this year’s edition?

We had a lot of chats about what we were going to do to mark this occasion. And the more I thought about it, the more I really started to think about the genesis of the festival. It was really always set up to be a showcase, a best-of-the-festivals model. For 70 years, the festival has brought really the best of the year in cinema to audiences. And especially now, we also have a little bit of a preview into the next six months of cinema.
points: Kristy Matheson previews key highlights and stars featured in the 70th edition and why she doesn't agree with people having "a grumble about how it doesn't seem like a big or a good year for cinema."

articles.title: John Oliver Has Re-Acquired Russell Crowe’s Iconic Jock Strap
articles.summary: This marks the third time the undergarment, which Crowe wore in 2005's 'Cinderella Man,' has been in the possession of the 'Last Week Tonight' host.
body: Russell Crowe ‘s jock strap is back in John Oliver’s possession once again.
This marks the third time the Last Week Tonight host has taken ownership of the undergarment that Crowe wore in 2005’s Cinderella Man.
Here’s the backstory: In 1028, Oliver bought the item at an auction Crowe called “The Art of the Divorce.” He put up more than 200 items for sale in the wake of his divorce from Danielle Spencer.

“It was my jock strap when I won the heavyweight championship of the world as the character James J. Braddock in the film Cinderella Man, ” he said. “I put it in the collection as a piece of whimsy and a bit of a gag. Funny enough, it’s garnered a lot of attention.”
